title: The Marathon and the Wall
subtitle: At about thirty kilometres, something happens that no amount of willpower prevents.
description: A B2 reading and listening text about the marathon: the physiology of 'the wall', why it happens where it does, and what runners do about it.
source: authored for this site; no source document
passage: Runners call it the wall, and the name is accurate. It arrives somewhere between thirty and thirty-five kilometres, and it does not feel like ordinary tiredness. The legs stop answering. The pace falls by a minute a kilometre or more, and no amount of willpower reverses it.

What is happening is simple enough to explain and very hard to avoid. The body stores carbohydrate as glycogen, in the muscles and the liver, and a trained adult holds perhaps two thousand calories of it. A marathon costs somewhere near two thousand six hundred. The arithmetic is the whole problem: at racing pace you run out before the finish.

Fat is the alternative fuel and there is plenty of it — even a lean runner carries enough for several marathons. But fat is metabolised more slowly, and it needs more oxygen for the same energy. When glycogen runs low the body switches over, and the switch is what the runner feels: the same effort now produces a slower pace. Worse, the brain depends on glucose, so the mental symptoms arrive with the physical ones. Runners describe losing the thread of simple arithmetic, misreading their own watch, and in bad cases a strange emotional flatness.

Three things postpone it. The first is pacing. Running the first half too fast burns glycogen disproportionately, because the faster you go the greater the share of energy that comes from carbohydrate rather than fat. Most people who hit the wall at thirty kilometres caused it at ten.

The second is fuelling during the race. Taking in thirty to sixty grams of carbohydrate an hour does not replace what is being spent, but it extends the supply. The practical difficulty is that the stomach tolerates much less at racing effort than at rest, which is why fuelling has to be rehearsed in training rather than attempted for the first time on the day.

The third is the training itself. Long slow runs improve the body's ability to use fat at a given pace, which spares glycogen, and they increase how much glycogen can be stored. This adaptation takes months and is the least glamorous part of a training plan.

What does not work is willpower alone. This is the part that surprises people, because the marathon has a century of literature attached to it about mental strength, and at thirty-two kilometres with no glycogen left the mind is simply not the limiting factor. A runner can want it enormously and still slow by fifteen per cent. The useful mental skill is narrower and less romantic: recognising the early signs, accepting the slower pace immediately rather than fighting it for two kilometres and paying for it, and continuing to take fuel when the stomach has stopped wanting any.

Elite runners hit the wall less often, and not because they suffer better. They have larger glycogen stores, use fat more efficiently, have practised their fuelling to the gram, and — most of all — pace the first half with a discipline that looks conservative to anyone watching. The wall is not a test of character. It is a budget, and the people who avoid it are the ones who did the arithmetic beforehand.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Several answers depend on the numbers. Read them carefully.

items.prompt: Where does the wall usually arrive?
What is the basic arithmetic of the problem?
options: A runner stores about 2,000 calories of glycogen and a marathon costs about 2,600
The race is longer than the body expects
items.explanation: “at racing pace you run out before the finish.”

items.prompt: Why does switching to fat slow a runner down?
options: Fat is metabolised more slowly and needs more oxygen for the same energy
There is not enough fat available
items.explanation: Even a lean runner carries enough fat for several marathons; the problem is the rate.

items.prompt: Why do mental symptoms appear alongside the physical ones?
items.explanation: Hence losing the thread of arithmetic and misreading a watch.

items.prompt: What does the author mean by “caused it at ten”?
options: Going out too fast early burns glycogen disproportionately
The wall begins at ten kilometres
items.explanation: The faster the pace, the greater the share of energy from carbohydrate.

items.prompt: Why must fuelling be practised in training?
options: The stomach tolerates much less at racing effort than at rest
items.explanation: “rather than attempted for the first time on the day.”

items.prompt: What do long slow runs achieve?
options: Better fat use at a given pace and greater glycogen storage

items.prompt: What is the author's view of mental strength here?
options: It is not the limiting factor once glycogen is gone
It is the most important factor
It matters only for elite runners
items.explanation: “A runner can want it enormously and still slow by fifteen per cent.”

items.prompt: What is the useful mental skill, according to the text?
options: Noticing early signs, accepting the slower pace at once, and continuing to fuel

items.prompt: Why do elite runners hit the wall less often?
options: Bigger stores, better fat use, rehearsed fuelling and disciplined early pacing
items.explanation: “The wall is not a test of character. It is a budget.”

exercises.title: Physiology and Pacing
exercises.instructions: Choose the word that fits the meaning.

items.prompt: The form the body stores carbohydrate in is ___.
items.explanation: Glucose is the circulating sugar; glycogen is the store.

items.prompt: To use less of something so that it lasts is to ___ it.
The one thing that decides how far you can go is the ___.
items.explanation: The author argues the mind is not it.

items.prompt: Much more than the size of the cause would suggest is ___.
items.explanation: Fast early running burns glycogen disproportionately.

items.prompt: A lasting change the body makes in response to training is an ___.
items.explanation: It takes months and is the least glamorous part of a plan.
How elite first-half pacing looks to a spectator.

discussion: Have you ever run out of energy during exercise? What did it feel like?
The author says the wall is a budget, not a test of character. Do you agree?
Where else in life do people blame willpower for an arithmetic problem?
What would you have to rehearse in advance for something you are planning?
Write about 250 words on a time you paced something badly at the start.
